The first three Gospels have so much in common that they are often called the Synoptic Gospels, from a Greek word meaning seen together. ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ stands apart. It begins not in ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧ or at the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, but before creation itself: in the beginning was the Word. Most of what it records appears nowhere else. There is no Sermon on the Mount, no parable of the sower, no casting out of demons. Instead there are long conversations, with a Pharisee by night, with a Samaritan woman at a well, with crowds and critics in the temple courts, and an extended farewell to the disciples on the night before the cross.

The Gospel rests on the testimony of the disciple whom ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ loved, who leans against Jesus at the last supper, stands at the cross, and runs to the empty tomb, and its closing lines say that this disciple wrote these things. He is ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, the son of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧, one of the twelve, who lived to a great age in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, the leading city of the Roman province of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧. Irenaeus, a bishop who as a young man had known Polycarp, a disciple of John, bears early witness to this. The Gospel's last verses add the voice of those around him: we know that his testimony is true. It was the last of the four Gospels to be written, toward the end of the first century.

⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ tells his readers plainly why he wrote: so that they may believe that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing they may have life in his name. He often explains Hebrew and Aramaic words, Rabbi, Messiah, ⟦l:siloam_1096|Siloam⟧, and Jewish customs and feasts, for many of his first readers lived far from ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧. Yet the book is steeped in the Scriptures and the worship of Israel, and it knows the geography of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and the land in close detail. It also reflects a painful separation, for it speaks of believers being put out of the synagogue. John often uses the phrase the Jews for the religious authorities in Jerusalem who oppose Jesus, rather than for the Jewish people as a whole, to which Jesus himself and every one of his first disciples belonged.

The other Gospels concentrate on ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, with a single climactic journey to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ at the end. ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ moves back and forth. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes up to Jerusalem again and again for the great festivals of the Jewish year, and the calendar gives the book much of its structure. There is a Passover near the beginning, an unnamed feast, a second Passover in Galilee, the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, the winter Feast of Dedication, and finally the last Passover, when he dies. Because John mentions three Passovers, it is from his Gospel that we know of a ministry of about three years. Again and again Jesus' words take up the images of the festival he is attending: the bread of the Passover, the water and light of Tabernacles.

⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ calls ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' miracles signs, because they point beyond themselves. He records only a handful of them, seven by the usual count before the resurrection, from water turned into wine at a wedding to a dead man called out of his tomb. Alongside them come the sayings that begin with the words I am: I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, the true vine. Those words carried a deep resonance for Jewish hearers, because I am echoes the name God gave himself to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ at the burning bush. John's vocabulary is simple and his ideas profound. He writes about light and darkness, life and death, truth and falsehood, believing and seeing, and his characters often misunderstand Jesus, taking literally what he means in a deeper sense.

The book moves in two great halves. After a prologue, the first twelve chapters follow ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' public ministry, his signs and his debates with the authorities, with growing belief on one side and hardening opposition on the other. Through these chapters runs a refrain, that his hour has not yet come. Then, as the last Passover approaches, Jesus says that the hour has come. The second half slows dramatically. Five chapters are given to a single evening, as Jesus washes his disciples' feet, speaks with them at length, and prays for them. Then come the arrest in a garden across the ⟦l:kidron_687|Kidron⟧ valley, the hearings before ⟦p:annas_269|Annas⟧ and ⟦p:caiaphas_532|Caiaphas⟧ and ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧, the crucifixion, and the first day of the week, when ⟦p:mary_1943|Mary Magdalene⟧ finds the tomb empty. A final chapter returns to the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧, with a breakfast on the shore and a conversation between the risen Jesus and ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧.

Readers who know the other Gospels will find ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ both familiar and new. The cast is the same: ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ and ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧, the sons of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧, ⟦p:caiaphas_532|Caiaphas⟧, ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧. But disciples who are little more than names elsewhere, ⟦p:philip_2344|Philip⟧ and ⟦p:thomas_2851|Thomas⟧, speak and question here, and others step into the light only in John's pages: ⟦p:nathanael_2158|Nathanael⟧ under his fig tree, ⟦p:nicodemus_2204|Nicodemus⟧ coming by night, and ⟦p:lazarus_1812|Lazarus⟧ of ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧, with his sisters ⟦p:martha_1937|Martha⟧ and ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧. And at every turn John invites his readers to consider the question that the prologue answers from the start: who is this man, and where has he come from?
1:
⟦p:john_1676|John⟧'s Gospel opens with the first words of Genesis: in the beginning. Before anything was made, the Word was already there, with God, and the Word was God. Through him all things were made, and in him was life, a light shining in the darkness that the darkness has not overcome. For Jews, God's word had always been at work in creation; Greek thinkers spoke of the word, the logos, as the reason that ordered the universe. Then comes a sentence neither had imagined: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. This opening passage, the prologue, is like an overture, and its light and darkness, witness, belief and glory will all return.

Into the prologue steps ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧, though here he is simply called ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧, and his role is to be a witness. The narrative then begins at ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧ beyond the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, where priests and Levites sent from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ question him about who he is. John does not describe the baptism of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ itself. Instead, over several days, the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God, and his own disciples start to follow. ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧ brings his brother ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧. ⟦p:philip_2344|Philip⟧, from ⟦l:bethsaida_231|Bethsaida⟧, brings ⟦p:nathanael_2158|Nathanael⟧, who is doubtful that anything good can come from ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧.
2:
On the third day, a wedding takes place at ⟦l:cana_271|Cana⟧, a village in the hills of ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has come with his new disciples, and his mother is there. Village weddings could last for days, and running out of wine would have been a lasting embarrassment for the bridegroom's family. Standing nearby are six large stone jars, each holding twenty to thirty gallons, kept for the Jewish rites of purification. What happens next ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ calls the first of Jesus' signs, the miracles that reveal who he is.

After a short stay in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ for the Passover, the first of three Passovers that ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ mentions. In the temple courts, where cattle, sheep and doves were sold for sacrifice and money was changed for the temple tax, he makes a whip of cords and drives the traders out. The other Gospels tell of Jesus clearing the temple again in the last week of his life. The authorities demand a sign, and Jesus speaks of destroying the temple and raising it in three days. ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s rebuilding had already been going on for forty-six years.
3:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and many have been impressed by his signs. Now a visitor comes to him at night. ⟦p:nicodemus_2204|Nicodemus⟧ is a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, a member of the ruling council, and he addresses Jesus respectfully as a teacher come from God. ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ does not say why he comes at night, but darkness and light matter in this Gospel.

The conversation turns quickly to the need to be born again. The Greek word can mean both again and from above, and ⟦p:nicodemus_2204|Nicodemus⟧ takes it in the most literal way. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks of wind and Spirit, and recalls the bronze snake that ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ lifted up in the wilderness, from the book of Numbers. Then comes one of the most quoted sentences in the Bible, about God's love for the world.

The second half of the chapter moves to the Judean countryside, where ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' disciples are baptising. ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧ is still at work nearby, at Aenon near Salim, and has not yet been imprisoned. When his disciples complain that the crowds are going to Jesus, he gives his answer with an image from a wedding.
4:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ leaves ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ to return to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, and he takes the direct route north through ⟦l:samaria_1022|Samaria⟧. The Samaritans were descended from the old northern kingdom of Israel and the peoples settled among them by the Assyrians. They accepted only the five books of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and worshipped on ⟦l:mount_gerizim_836|Mount Gerizim⟧, where their temple had stood until a Hasmonean king destroyed it. Jews and Samaritans had kept apart, often bitterly, for centuries.

At midday, tired from the road, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ sits by ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧'s well near the town of Sychar, close to ancient Shechem and within sight of ⟦l:mount_gerizim_836|Mount Gerizim⟧, near the plot of ground Jacob gave to his son ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧. His disciples have gone into the town to buy food. A Samaritan woman comes to draw water, and Jesus asks her for a drink. For a Jewish teacher to speak with her at all was extraordinary, as both she and his returning disciples recognise. Their conversation moves from well water to living water, and from her own life to the long dispute over where God should be worshipped.

After two days among the Samaritans, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to ⟦l:cana_271|Cana⟧. A royal official in the service of ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧ comes from ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, some distance away by the lake, to plead for his dying son. This is the second sign.
5:
Some time later there is another feast, which ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ does not name, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ again. Near the ⟦l:sheep_gate_1070|Sheep Gate⟧, north of the temple, is a pool called ⟦l:bethesda_205|Bethesda⟧, surrounded by five covered colonnades. Archaeologists have uncovered a pair of large pools on that site, with porticoes around and between them. The sick lie there in great numbers, waiting for the water to be stirred.

One man has been an invalid for thirty-eight years. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ tells him to pick up his mat and walk, and he does. But it is the Sabbath, and carrying a mat counts as work. The authorities challenge the man, and then Jesus himself.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' reply, my Father is working until now, and I am working, makes matters far worse. His hearers understand him to be making himself equal with God, and now, ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ says, they try all the harder to kill him. The rest of the chapter is a long answer, as if in a courtroom, about the Son's relationship to the Father and the witnesses who support his claims: ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧, the works he does, the Father himself, and the Scriptures, including the writings of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧.
6:
The scene moves back to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, to the far side of the lake, which ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ also calls the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Tiberias⟧, after the city ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧ had built on its western shore and named for the emperor. It is spring, and the Passover is near. A large crowd has followed ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ up onto the hillside.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle before the resurrection told in all four Gospels, and ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ adds details of his own: ⟦p:philip_2344|Philip⟧'s reckoning that two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread, and ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧'s discovery of a boy with five barley loaves, the bread of the poor. Afterwards the crowd wants to seize ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ and make him king, and he withdraws. That night the disciples, rowing across to ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧ in a strong wind, see him walking on the water.

The next day, in the synagogue at ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, the crowd catches up with him, and the rest of the chapter is a long discussion about bread. They remember the manna in the wilderness, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks of himself as the bread of life. His words are hard to accept, and many disciples turn away. Jesus asks the twelve whether they will leave too, and ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ answers for them.
7:
Six months have passed since the Passover of the previous chapter. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has kept to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, because the authorities in ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ want to kill him. Now the Feast of Tabernacles is near, the great autumn festival at the end of the harvest, when Jews lived for a week in shelters made of branches to recall Israel's years in the wilderness. ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ would be crowded with pilgrims.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' brothers, who do not yet believe in him, urge him to go up and show himself. He refuses, but later goes up privately, and halfway through the feast he begins to teach openly in the temple courts. The city is divided about him, and the debates turn on his learning, on the Sabbath healing from chapter five, and on where the Messiah would come from.

Each day of the feast, water was carried in procession up from the ⟦l:siloam_1096|Pool of Siloam⟧ and poured out at the altar. On the last and greatest day, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ stands and cries out, if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me. The chief priests send officers to arrest him, and they come back empty-handed. ⟦p:nicodemus_2204|Nicodemus⟧, who came to Jesus by night, speaks up cautiously for him.
8:
The leaders' argument is over, everyone has gone home, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ has spent the night on the ⟦l:mount_of_olives_861|Mount of Olives⟧. Early in the morning he is back in the temple courts, seated and teaching the people, when scribes and Pharisees bring in a woman caught in adultery and make her stand before them all. They want to trap him.

Then the teaching in the temple resumes, still in the setting of the feast. During Tabernacles great lamps were lit in the temple courts, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, teaching near the treasury, declares, I am the light of the world. What follows is the sharpest debate in the Gospel so far. Jesus speaks of truth that sets people free, and his hearers protest that they are ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧'s descendants and have never been slaves of anyone. The argument turns on who their true father is.

The exchange rises to a final claim: before ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ was born, I am. Those words echo the name God revealed to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and the listeners understand them. They pick up stones to throw at him, but ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ slips away from the temple.
9:
Still in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ and his disciples pass a man who has been blind from birth. The disciples ask a question that reflects a common belief of the time, that suffering must be the result of someone's sin: was it this man's, or his parents'? Jesus answers that it is neither, and that this has happened so that the works of God may be displayed in him. Then he repeats what he said at the feast: he is the light of the world.

He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash in the ⟦l:siloam_1096|Pool of Siloam⟧, at the southern end of the city. ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ notes that the name means sent. The man comes back seeing. Once again the healing takes place on the Sabbath, and making mud counted as work.

What follows is told almost like a trial, in a series of scenes. Neighbours argue about whether this is really the same man. The Pharisees question him, then his parents, who are afraid to say much, because anyone who confessed ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ as the Christ was to be put out of the synagogue. Then they question the man again. As the pressure grows, so does his boldness. The chapter ends with Jesus finding him, and with words about who is truly blind.
10:
There is no break between the previous chapter and this one. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still speaking to the Pharisees who questioned the man born blind, and he turns to an image every Judean knew: a sheepfold, a shepherd, and sheep that know his voice. The Scriptures had long pictured Israel's leaders as shepherds and condemned those who failed the flock. Jesus calls himself the gate for the sheep and the good shepherd, who lays down his life for them. Once again his listeners are divided.

Then ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ moves the story on to the end of the year. It is winter, and the Feast of Dedication is being held in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. This is Hanukkah, the festival that remembers the cleansing and rededication of the temple by Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, after it had been defiled by the Syrian king Antiochus. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is walking in ⟦p:solomon_2762|Solomon⟧'s Colonnade, a covered walkway along the eastern side of the temple courts.

The leaders surround him and demand that he tell them plainly whether he is the Christ. His answer ends with the words, I and the Father are one, and again they take up stones. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ withdraws across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, to the place where ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ had first baptised, and many there believe in him.
11:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is staying across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ when a message arrives from ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧, a village less than two miles from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ on the far side of the ⟦l:mount_of_olives_861|Mount of Olives⟧. ⟦p:lazarus_1812|Lazarus⟧ is ill. He and his sisters, ⟦p:martha_1937|Martha⟧ and ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧, are close friends, and ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ says plainly that Jesus loved them. Yet he stays where he is two more days, and when he sets out, his disciples are alarmed that he means to go back to ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ so soon after he was nearly stoned. ⟦p:thomas_2851|Thomas⟧, called ⟦p:thomas_2851|Didymus⟧, the twin, speaks up with grim loyalty.

By the time ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ arrives, ⟦p:lazarus_1812|Lazarus⟧ has been in the tomb for four days. Each sister meets Jesus with the same words of grief. To ⟦p:martha_1937|Martha⟧ he says, I am the resurrection and the life. At the tomb, a cave with a stone across its entrance, the shortest verse in the Bible records that Jesus wept.

By the usual count this is the seventh and greatest of the signs before the cross, and its consequences are immediate. The chief priests and Pharisees call a meeting of the Sanhedrin, fearing that the Romans will come and take away both their place and their nation. ⟦p:caiaphas_532|Caiaphas⟧, the high priest that year, gives his counsel, and from that day they plan to kill ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. Jesus withdraws to a town called ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, near the wilderness, as the Passover approaches.
12:
Six days before the Passover, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧, and a dinner is given in his honour, with ⟦p:lazarus_1812|Lazarus⟧ at the table and ⟦p:martha_1937|Martha⟧ serving. ⟦p:mary_1939|Mary⟧ pours a pint of costly perfume of pure nard on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ tell of an anointing at Bethany by an unnamed woman; ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ names her, and adds that ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas⟧, who kept the money bag, was a thief. The chief priests now plan to kill Lazarus too.

The next day ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ enters ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Only ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ mentions that the crowds carried palm branches, which had been a symbol of Jewish national victory since the days of the Maccabees. They hail him as the King of Israel.

Then some Greeks who have come up to worship at the feast ask ⟦p:philip_2344|Philip⟧ if they may see ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. This is the moment Jesus has spoken of since ⟦l:cana_271|Cana⟧. The hour has come, he says, and he speaks of a grain of wheat that must fall into the ground and die. A voice comes from heaven. The chapter closes the first half of the Gospel, with ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧'s reflection, drawn from ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧, on why so many did not believe, and with Jesus' last public words.
13:
The second half of the Gospel begins, and the pace slows almost to a halt. Chapters thirteen to seventeen all belong to one evening, the last before ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' death. It is just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knows that his hour has come to leave this world and return to the Father. The evening meal is under way, and ⟦p:satan_2476|the devil⟧ has already put into the heart of ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas⟧ the intention to betray him.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ gets up from the table, ties a towel around his waist and washes his disciples' feet. On dusty roads in sandals, feet got filthy, and washing them was a job for the lowest servant. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ at first refuses to allow it.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ becomes troubled and says that one of them will betray him. Here, for the first time, ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ mentions the disciple whom Jesus loved, reclining next to him. Guests at a formal meal lay on couches around a low table, so he can lean back and ask Jesus quietly who it is. ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas⟧ takes the piece of bread Jesus offers and goes out, and John adds four words: and it was night. Jesus then gives his disciples a new commandment, and warns ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ that before the rooster crows he will deny him three times.
14:
Judas has gone out into the night, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is alone at the table with the eleven. He has just told them that he is going where they cannot follow, and that ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ will deny him. They are shaken. This chapter begins what is often called the farewell discourse, which runs through chapter sixteen and closes with the prayer of chapter seventeen.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ begins by telling them not to let their hearts be troubled, and speaks of his Father's house with its many rooms. The talk moves forward through the questions of individual disciples, each of whom reveals how little they yet understand. ⟦p:thomas_2851|Thomas⟧ says they do not know the way, ⟦p:philip_2344|Philip⟧ asks Jesus to show them the Father, and another Judas, not Iscariot, asks why Jesus will reveal himself to them and not to the world.

For the first time ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ promises another Advocate, the Holy Spirit. The Greek word, Paraclete, means one called alongside to help, and it could be used of a counsel for the defence. The chapter ends with the words, get up, let us go on from here. Yet the teaching continues for three more chapters before they cross the ⟦l:kidron_687|Kidron⟧ valley.
15:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still speaking to the eleven on the last night. He now uses one of the oldest images of Israel in the Scriptures, the vine. Psalms and prophets had pictured God's people as a vine he planted and tended, which too often bore no good fruit. Over the entrance to the sanctuary of ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s temple hung a great golden vine. Jesus says, I am the true vine, and his Father is the vinedresser, and he describes the disciples as branches, who can bear fruit only by remaining in him.

From the vine he moves to love. He has loved them as the Father has loved him, and he calls them no longer servants but friends. The greatest love, he says, is to lay down one's life for one's friends, words spoken only hours before his death.

The mood then darkens. The world that has hated him will hate them too, and he tells them to expect it. The chapter closes with a second promise of the Advocate, ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of truth, who will testify about him, as the disciples themselves will, because they have been with him from the beginning.
16:
The farewell discourse continues, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks frankly about what lies ahead for his followers. They will be put out of the synagogues, and a time will come when those who kill them will think they are serving God. He says he is telling them now, so that when it happens they will remember.

The disciples are filled with grief at the thought of his going away, but ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ insists it is for their good, because only then will the Advocate come. He describes what ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ will do, both in the world and among the disciples, guiding them into all truth.
